claims.text: Tuning the coordination environment of noble-metal precursors can synchronize their reduction kinetics.
Synchronized reduction kinetics produce simultaneous metal-atom release.
Nearly concurrent nucleation enables formation of homogeneous high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Nearly concurrent nucleation produces nanoparticles with substantial surface-atom exposure.
Asynchronous reduction causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Ligand coordination modifies precursor stability and metal-ion release rates.
Metal-ion release rate dictates the temporal distribution of nucleation events.
The temporal distribution of nucleation events determines whether nanoparticles become uniformly alloyed or segregated.
Staggered metal-atom release causes sequential nucleation.
Sequential nucleation leads to elemental segregation, phase separation, and potentially non-uniform morphology.
An optimized coordination environment will yield a narrower particle-size distribution than a conventional ligand environment.
A conventional ligand environment will yield nanoparticles with lower catalytic surface exposure than the tailored environment.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles made by solution-phase reduction when ligand coordination can modulate precursor-reduction kinetics.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to routes dominated by purely thermal or substrate-induced mechanisms.
